title: Cookies - setcookie, reading, and secure flags
answer: Set a cookie with setcookie before any output. Read it on later requests from $_COOKIE. Mark cookies HttpOnly so JavaScript cannot read them, Secure so they only travel over HTTPS, and SameSite=Lax to reduce cross-site request forgery. Never store passwords or secrets in a cookie.
pitfall: A cookie set during this request is not visible in $_COOKIE until the next request. Reading it immediately after setcookie returns the old value.

title: Request info from $_SERVER - method, path, IP, and user agent
answer: $_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'] tells you GET or POST, REQUEST_URI gives the requested path, and REMOTE_ADDR gives the client IP. Build the current URL from the host and URI, but never trust the Host header for security decisions, because the client controls it.
pitfall: REMOTE_ADDR is the last proxy's address when a load balancer or CDN sits in front of your app. Behind a proxy, check the forwarded headers your proxy documents, and only trust headers your own proxy sets.

title: Sessions - login state with $_SESSION
answer: Call session_start before any output, then store login state in $_SESSION. Regenerate the session ID after login to prevent session fixation. Destroy the session and its cookie on logout. This example is syntax-checked only because sessions need an HTTP request.
pitfall: Calling session_start after echoing HTML triggers 'headers already sent'. Start the session at the very top of the script, before any output.

title: Superglobals - $_GET, $_POST, $_SERVER, $_REQUEST, $_ENV
answer: $_GET holds URL parameters, $_POST holds form data, $_SERVER holds request and server details, and $_ENV holds environment variables. Avoid $_REQUEST because it merges sources and hides where a value came from. Read every superglobal value with ?? or isset, never directly.
pitfall: Trusting $_GET or $_POST values without validation is the root of most PHP security bugs. Treat every superglobal value as untrusted input.
